scenarios.title: Planning Your Study Path
scenarios.situation: You have 3 weeks before your DP-203: Azure Data Engineer interview/exam. You've just opened this bootcamp with 15 domains ahead of you.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most effective study sequence?
choices: Start Here lessons → core domains in order → Systems Anatomy → Mock Assessment → Capstone, doing drills daily
Jump straight to the Mock Assessment to see where you stand
Study only your weakest domain until it's perfect, then move on
Read all lessons first, then do all scenarios, then all labs
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The bootcamp is sequenced deliberately: orientation first, then progressive domain mastery with interleaved drills for retention, Systems Anatomy to connect it all, mock under realistic conditions, capstone to prove it. Jumping to the mock wastes its diagnostic value; perfecting one domain starves the others; batching by activity type kills interleaving benefits.
scenarios.hint: What does each phase prepare you for? What happens if you skip the foundation?

scenarios.title: The Passive Reader Trap
scenarios.situation: A learner has 'completed' 40 lessons but fails every scenario. They read each lesson carefully and passed all knowledge checks on the first try.
scenarios.prompt: What went wrong, and what's the fix?
choices: They consumed passively without application — the fix is interleaving scenarios immediately after lessons and doing teach-backs aloud
The lessons are too easy — skip to harder material
They need to re-read the lessons more carefully
Knowledge checks are broken — report a bug
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Passing knowledge checks proves recognition, not application. Scenarios demand transfer — using knowledge in novel situations. The fix is structural: never finish a lesson without immediately attempting its scenarios, and explain each concept aloud (teach-back) to expose shallow understanding.
scenarios.hint: What's the difference between recognizing an answer and producing one under pressure?

scenarios.title: The rename failure
scenarios.situation: A data lake on regular Blob storage can't atomically rename directories, breaking Spark job commits.
scenarios.prompt: What storage design fixes this?
choices: Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 — hierarchical namespace enables atomic directory operations for analytics engines
Premium page blobs
A file share
More containers
scenarios.why: ADLS Gen2's hierarchical namespace brings true directories with atomic renames — which Spark and Hadoop rely on for commit protocols. Flat blob namespaces emulate folders and can't guarantee atomic directory operations.
scenarios.hint: Which storage flavor gives you real directories with atomic renames?

scenarios.title: The CSV swamp
scenarios.situation: A lake stores everything as CSV. Queries scan full files, schemas drift, and there's no way to update a single record.
scenarios.prompt: What file format should the curated zone use?
choices: Parquet (columnar) — or Delta Lake on Parquet for ACID, time travel, and upserts
More CSV files
JSON lines for everything
Excel workbooks
scenarios.why: Parquet's columnar layout means queries read only needed columns (massive scan reduction); Delta Lake adds ACID transactions, schema enforcement, and time travel on top. CSV is the raw-landing format, not the curated-zone format.
scenarios.hint: Columnar reads plus transactions — which format family?

scenarios.title: The full-scan query
scenarios.situation: Analysts query a 50 TB sales table filtered by month, but every query scans all 50 TB.
scenarios.prompt: What physical design fixes this?
choices: Partitioning by date (e.g., year=/month= folders) — partition pruning skips irrelevant data
A bigger Synapse pool
More indexes on CSV
Copying the table per analyst
scenarios.why: Partitioning organizes data so the engine prunes (skips) partitions outside the filter — a month query reads 1/60th of 5 years. Without partitioning, every query pays the full-scan price.
scenarios.hint: How do you make a month-filtered query skip the other 59 months?

scenarios.title: The medallion
scenarios.situation: Raw feeds land in all shapes; analysts need clean, conformed tables; data scientists want feature-ready aggregates.
scenarios.prompt: What zone design organizes this?
choices: Medallion architecture — Bronze (raw), Silver (cleaned/conformed), Gold (aggregated/business-ready)
One zone for everything
Bronze only
A relational database instead
scenarios.why: Medallion (bronze/silver/gold) structures the lake by refinement: immutable raw landing, validated conformed data, then business aggregates. Each layer has clear quality contracts and consumers.
scenarios.hint: Raw, cleaned, business-ready — what are the three layers called?

scenarios.title: The hot raw data
scenarios.situation: Raw landing data stays on Hot tier forever though nobody reads landings older than 90 days.
scenarios.prompt: What automates tiering?
choices: Lifecycle management policies — e.g., Hot→Cool at 90 days, →Archive at 365
Manual tier changes quarterly
Deleting raw data after 90 days
A bigger storage account
scenarios.why: Lifecycle policies automate tier transitions by age/last-access — the cost control for append-only lake landings. Archive tier suits compliance retention; Cool suits occasional reprocessing.
scenarios.hint: How do you age data down the tiers automatically?

scenarios.title: The million tiny files
scenarios.situation: Streaming ingestion writes one small JSON file per event — 2 million files a day. Spark jobs now take hours just listing files.
scenarios.prompt: What is the problem and fix?
choices: Small-file problem — compact/merge files (auto-compaction, streaming checkpoints with larger triggers) to right-size files
More Spark executors
A bigger driver node
Faster storage
scenarios.why: Analytics engines pay per-file overhead (listing, opening, metadata); millions of tiny files destroy performance. Compaction merges them into optimally-sized files (hundreds of MB); streaming sinks should batch appropriately.
scenarios.hint: Millions of tiny files kill Spark. What file hygiene fixes it?

scenarios.title: The hardcoded server
scenarios.situation: Fifty pipelines hardcode the SQL server name. A migration to a new server means editing all fifty.
scenarios.prompt: What ADF design centralizes connection info?
choices: Linked services — define the connection once; datasets and pipelines reference it
Copying the JSON fifty times
A variable per pipeline
Hardcoding the new name
scenarios.why: Linked services encapsulate connection information (server, auth via managed identity/Key Vault) as reusable named resources. Change the server once in the linked service — all fifty pipelines follow.
scenarios.hint: Where should connection details live so fifty pipelines share one definition?

scenarios.title: The on-prem source
scenarios.situation: A pipeline must copy data from an on-premises SQL Server behind the corporate firewall — no inbound ports allowed.
scenarios.prompt: Which integration runtime fits?
choices: Self-hosted IR — installed on-premises, makes outbound-only connections to ADF
Azure IR — can't reach behind the firewall
SSIS IR — for SSIS packages, not this
A VPN gateway alone
scenarios.why: The self-hosted integration runtime runs inside your network and initiates outbound connections to Data Factory — no inbound firewall rules. Azure IR handles cloud sources; SSIS IR lifts SSIS packages.
scenarios.hint: Which IR reaches on-premises data without inbound firewall rules?

scenarios.title: The legacy packages
scenarios.situation: The company has 300 SSIS packages with complex logic that must run in Azure with minimal rewrite.
scenarios.prompt: What runs them natively?
choices: Azure-SSIS integration runtime — lift-and-shift SSIS execution in ADF
Rewriting all 300 as ADF pipelines immediately
Azure IR alone
A VM per package
scenarios.why: The SSIS IR provisions the SSIS engine in ADF so existing packages run with minimal change — the pragmatic bridge while teams modernize package by package.
scenarios.hint: Which IR executes existing SSIS packages in the cloud?

scenarios.title: The late file
scenarios.situation: A daily pipeline runs at 6 AM but the source file sometimes arrives at 7 AM, processing yesterday's file again.
scenarios.prompt: What trigger reacts to the file's arrival?
choices: An event-based trigger on BlobCreated — runs when the file lands, not on a clock
A schedule trigger at 6 AM
A manual trigger
A tumbling window trigger
scenarios.why: Event triggers fire on storage events (BlobCreated/Deleted) so pipelines run on data arrival, not on a possibly-wrong schedule. Schedule triggers assume timeliness; event triggers react to reality.
scenarios.hint: What fires the pipeline when the file actually arrives?

scenarios.title: The no-code transform
scenarios.situation: Analysts need to join, aggregate, and clean data visually without writing Spark code.
scenarios.prompt: What ADF feature provides this?
choices: Mapping data flows — visual transformations executed on Spark clusters
Copy activity — moves data without transforming
A notebook
The portal's data preview
scenarios.why: Mapping data flows give a visual designer for joins, aggregations, window functions, and schema handling, executed on ADF-managed Spark — ETL for teams that think in diagrams, with code (wraggle/data flow script) underneath.
scenarios.hint: Visual transformations on Spark without writing Spark — which feature?

scenarios.title: The ten environments
scenarios.situation: Pipelines must run in dev, test, and prod with different servers and containers, but the team maintains three copies of each pipeline.
scenarios.prompt: What eliminates the copies?
choices: Parameterization — pipeline/linked-service parameters fed per environment (ARM template parameters or global parameters)
Three copies forever
Hardcoding per environment
One environment for all
scenarios.why: Parameters let one pipeline definition run anywhere: linked services and datasets take parameters resolved at runtime or deploy time. One definition, N environments — the DRY principle for data engineering.
scenarios.hint: How does one pipeline run against dev, test, and prod?

scenarios.title: The predictable warehouse
scenarios.situation: A retailer runs heavy, predictable nightly ETL plus daytime BI on 20 TB — needs reserved, consistent performance.
scenarios.prompt: Which Synapse SQL option fits?
choices: Dedicated SQL pool — provisioned DWUs for predictable, heavy workloads
Serverless SQL pool — pay-per-query, for ad-hoc exploration
Spark pool — for the SQL ETL
Cosmos DB
scenarios.why: Dedicated SQL pools provision compute (DWUs) for consistent, heavy relational workloads — the classic data warehouse. Serverless is pay-per-TB-scanned for ad-hoc queries over the lake; neither replaces the other.
scenarios.hint: Predictable heavy SQL with provisioned performance — which pool?

scenarios.title: The ad-hoc analyst
scenarios.situation: An analyst occasionally queries Parquet files in the lake with T-SQL — a few queries a week, no ETL.
scenarios.prompt: Which option is most economical?
choices: Serverless SQL pool — pay per TB scanned, no infrastructure to manage
Dedicated SQL pool running 24/7
A Spark cluster always on
Copying Parquet into SQL Server
scenarios.why: Serverless SQL pools charge per data scanned with zero provisioning — ideal for sporadic analyst queries over lake files. Running dedicated capacity for a few queries a week is pure waste.
scenarios.hint: Occasional T-SQL over lake files — which pool charges only per query?

scenarios.title: The skewed join
scenarios.situation: A Spark job joining a 2 TB fact table to a 50 MB dimension table shuffles for hours.
scenarios.prompt: What optimization applies?
choices: Broadcast the small dimension table — send it to all executors, avoiding the shuffle
More executors
A bigger driver
Repartitioning the fact table randomly
scenarios.why: Broadcast joins replicate the small table to every executor so the big table isn't shuffled — the standard fix for fact-to-small-dimension joins. Shuffling 2 TB to co-locate keys is the cost being avoided.
scenarios.hint: Small dimension, huge fact — how do you avoid shuffling the huge side?

scenarios.title: The bad load
scenarios.situation: A bad ETL load corrupts the Delta table. The team needs yesterday's correct data back.
scenarios.prompt: What Delta Lake feature recovers it?
choices: Time travel — query/restore the table as of a previous version/timestamp
Re-running the whole history
The recycle bin
A database backup from last month
scenarios.why: Delta Lake versions every transaction; time travel (VERSION AS OF / TIMESTAMP AS OF) queries or restores prior versions — the built-in undo for bad loads. It's ACID transactions plus history, not just files.
scenarios.hint: What lets you query the table as it looked yesterday?

scenarios.title: The shared exploration
scenarios.situation: Data scientists share analysis as email attachments of scripts; nobody can reproduce anyone's results.
scenarios.prompt: What Databricks practice fixes this?
choices: Notebooks with version control (Repos) — shared, reproducible, reviewable analysis
Emailing scripts
Screenshots of results
One giant shared script
scenarios.why: Databricks Repos bring notebooks under Git version control — shared, diffable, reproducible. Combined with cluster-scoped libraries and jobs, exploration becomes engineering instead of folklore.
scenarios.hint: How do notebooks become reproducible and reviewable?

scenarios.title: The arriving files
scenarios.situation: Thousands of files land in the lake daily; a Structured Streaming job must pick up new ones incrementally without listing the whole directory.
scenarios.prompt: What ingestion pattern fits?
choices: Auto Loader — incrementally processes new files as they arrive, tracking state
A batch job listing everything hourly
Manual file copies
A trigger per file
scenarios.why: Auto Loader (cloudFiles) uses event notifications or directory listing checkpoints to incrementally ingest new files — efficient, exactly-once-ish, schema-evolution-aware. Full directory scans don't scale with file counts.
scenarios.hint: How do you incrementally ingest thousands of new files a day?

scenarios.title: The ordered device stream
scenarios.situation: A million IoT devices send telemetry; each device's readings must be processed in order, scaled across consumers.
scenarios.prompt: How do Event Hubs partitions serve this?
choices: Partition by device ID — ordering guaranteed within a partition; consumer groups scale processing across partitions
One partition for everything
No partitions
A queue per device
scenarios.why: Event Hubs partitions are the unit of ordering and parallelism: same key → same partition → order preserved; more partitions → more parallel consumers. Partition key design is the core streaming decision.
scenarios.hint: What gives per-device ordering plus parallel consumption?

scenarios.title: The two readers
scenarios.situation: A real-time dashboard and a long-term archive both need every event from the same hub, at their own pace.
scenarios.prompt: What lets both read independently?
choices: Consumer groups — each gets its own offset/cursor over the partitions
Two event hubs with duplicated data
One reader sharing its offset
Polling the portal
scenarios.why: Consumer groups give each downstream app an independent view (own offsets) of the same partitions — the dashboard reads real-time while the archive lags, neither blocking the other. Duplicating the hub doubles cost for no reason.
scenarios.hint: How do two apps read the same stream at different speeds?

scenarios.title: The 5-minute average
scenarios.situation: A Stream Analytics job must compute each sensor's average temperature over hopping 5-minute windows.
scenarios.prompt: Which windowing applies?
evidence: SELECT sensorId, AVG(temp) FROM input TIMESTAMP BY eventTime GROUP BY sensorId, HoppingWindow(minute, 5, 1)
choices: A hopping (or tumbling) window of 5 minutes with GROUP BY sensor — windows define the aggregation scope
No window — stream jobs aggregate forever
A 5-minute VM
A batch job
scenarios.why: Stream Analytics windows (tumbling: non-overlapping; hopping: overlapping; sliding; session) bound aggregations in event time. The window choice defines exactly which events each average covers — the heart of stream SQL.
scenarios.hint: What bounds a 'last 5 minutes' aggregation in a stream?

scenarios.title: The delayed sensor
scenarios.situation: Sensors buffer readings offline and send them hours late; the stream job currently drops them silently.
scenarios.prompt: What handles late arrivals?
choices: Late-arrival tolerance and out-of-order policies — configure how late events are admitted vs. dropped
Ignoring the problem
A bigger window
Faster sensors
scenarios.why: Stream systems define lateness policies: how far behind event time you'll still accept data. Real devices go offline — the design must choose between dropping late data or accommodating it, explicitly.
scenarios.hint: Events arrive hours late. What policy decides their fate?

scenarios.title: The replay need
scenarios.situation: Compliance requires every raw event retained for 2 years and replayable into new analytics.
scenarios.prompt: What Event Hubs feature provides this?
choices: Capture — automatically writes raw events to ADLS/Blob in Avro/Parquet for replay and batch analysis
Consumer groups — don't retain raw files
A bigger retention period alone
Screenshots
scenarios.why: Event Hubs Capture lands the raw stream to storage (Avro/Parquet) continuously — the immutable raw record for compliance, replay, and batch reprocessing. Retention keeps events in the hub briefly; Capture archives them durably.
scenarios.hint: What archives the raw stream to the lake automatically?

scenarios.title: The downstream outage
scenarios.situation: The stream job's database sink goes down for an hour; events must not be lost and the job must catch up after.
scenarios.prompt: What property of the design saves the data?
choices: Durable buffered ingestion (Event Hubs retention) + checkpointing — the job resumes from the last checkpoint and replays
In-memory buffers only
Dropping events during outages
Restarting from scratch
scenarios.why: Event Hubs retains events for the configured period; streaming jobs checkpoint offsets, so after a sink outage they resume and catch up from the buffer. Durability lives in the log (the hub), not in the processor's memory.
scenarios.hint: Where does the data wait safely during a sink outage?

scenarios.title: The pipeline credential
scenarios.situation: ADF pipelines connect to SQL and Storage with stored passwords that expire and break nightly loads.
scenarios.prompt: What authentication should pipelines use?
choices: Managed identity for Data Factory — grant it data-plane roles on each source/sink; no stored passwords
Longer password expiry
The same password everywhere
A shared admin account
scenarios.why: ADF's system-assigned managed identity authenticates to Azure data stores via RBAC — no credentials to rotate, expire, or leak. Stored credentials in linked services are the fragile pattern this replaces.
scenarios.hint: How do pipelines authenticate with zero stored secrets?

scenarios.title: The public lake
scenarios.situation: The data lake's storage account allows public network access; auditors flag PII-adjacent datasets.
scenarios.prompt: What network controls apply?
choices: Private endpoints for the lake + storage firewall denying public access, with ADF/Synapse connecting privately
A longer SAS token
HTTPS only
A resource lock
scenarios.why: Data-plane privacy needs private endpoints (lake traffic stays in the VNet) plus public-access disabled at the account level. ADF needs a managed VNet/IR or private endpoints to reach it — network design is part of data security.
scenarios.hint: How do you make lake traffic never touch the public internet?

scenarios.title: The key control
scenarios.situation: A customer contract requires the company — not Microsoft — to control the encryption keys for their data lake.
scenarios.prompt: What satisfies this?
choices: Customer-managed keys (CMK) in Key Vault — Microsoft still encrypts, but key lifecycle is yours
Disabling encryption
A resource lock
Longer passwords
scenarios.why: CMK moves key control (creation, rotation, revocation) to your Key Vault while the service still performs encryption. Revoking the key renders the data unreadable — the contractual 'we control the keys' proof.
scenarios.hint: Who controls key lifecycle with CMK, and what does revocation do?

scenarios.title: The regional analysts
scenarios.situation: Analysts in each region must see only their region's rows in a shared sales table.
scenarios.prompt: What enforces this in the warehouse?
choices: Row-level security — filter predicates by user/region so one table serves all with scoped visibility
Separate tables per region
Trusting analysts not to look
Deleting other regions' data
scenarios.why: RLS applies security predicates (e.g., WHERE region = USER's region) transparently — one table, per-user visibility. It's the standard multi-tenant analytics pattern, enforced by the engine, not by convention.
scenarios.hint: One table, each user sees only their rows — which feature?

scenarios.title: The unknown PII
scenarios.situation: Nobody knows which lake datasets contain customer emails; a privacy request is due in 72 hours.
scenarios.prompt: What finds the PII fast?
choices: Microsoft Purview scans with classification rules — auto-labels PII across the lake with a searchable catalog
Manual file opening
Asking each team
A bigger lake
scenarios.why: Purview's scanners classify sensitive data (emails, SSNs, etc.) across ADLS, SQL, and more, building a searchable data map — the only feasible answer at lake scale under a deadline.
scenarios.hint: What scans the whole lake and labels sensitive data automatically?

scenarios.title: The suspicious query
scenarios.situation: A DBA needs a tamper-evident record of who queried the finance database and when.
scenarios.prompt: What provides this?
choices: SQL auditing — logs database events to Log Analytics/Storage for forensic review
The application logs
Trusting the DBA's memory
Disabling the database
scenarios.why: Azure SQL Auditing records database events (logins, queries, permission changes) to immutable storage — the compliance trail for 'who touched the data'. Application logs see app behavior, not direct database access.
scenarios.hint: Which feature logs database access for forensics?

lessons.title: Azure Data Engineer — Core concepts
concepts: Ingestion has two shapes: batch (Data Factory orchestrates scheduled movement, minutes-to-hours latency) and streaming (Event Hubs ingests continuous events for seconds-level processing) — pick by required freshness.
Incremental loading beats full reloads: watermark columns (or change tracking) extract only new/changed rows, turning O(table) nightly jobs into O(delta) ones.
Partitioning and columnar storage make big tables fast: partition elimination and columnstore segment pruning let queries skip data they don't need — fix layout before scaling compute.
Event Hubs scales on two axes: throughput units for ingress/egress and partitions for consumer parallelism; each consumer app needs its own consumer group plus offset checkpointing to resume cleanly.
Synapse offers serverless SQL (pay per query, ideal for ad-hoc lake exploration) and dedicated SQL pools (provisioned compute for heavy predictable ETL, pausable) — match pool to workload shape.
Medallion architecture layers responsibility: bronze keeps raw landed data (schema-on-read absorbs source drift), silver cleans and conforms, gold serves stable analytics contracts.

  --name orders --partition-count 8 --message-retention 1
example.walkthrough: Create a Standard Event Hubs namespace, then an event hub with 8 partitions and 1-day retention. Partition count sets the parallelism ceiling for consumers — size it to the number of consumer instances you plan to run.

Common trap: sharing one consumer group across apps — they steal each other's offsets; each app needs its own group plus checkpointing.

example.walkthrough: Draft your resume bullet and demo opener now, even before the project is done. They'll sharpen as you build.

pitfalls: Demoing without a narrative — clicking around silently while the interviewer watches is painful.
No answer for 'what would you do differently' — always have one; it shows growth mindset.
Portfolio link rot — verify every link on your resume actually works before submitting.
lessons.try_it: Record a 60-second screen share of your current progress. Watch it back — is the narrative clear?

lessons.title: DP-203 Exam Blueprint
concepts: Four domains: design/implement data storage (15-20%), develop data processing (40-45%), secure/monitor/optimize (30-35%) — weight your study accordingly
Question style: scenario-heavy ('you need to... which service?') — memorize decision criteria, not feature lists
Case studies: long scenarios with multiple questions — read questions first, then mine the case for answers
Hands-on beats reading: the exam rewards people who've actually built pipelines, not just watched videos

example.code:
Decision pattern: 'ingest 1M events/sec, <1min latency'
→ Event Hubs (not IoT Hub — no device mgmt needed)
→ Stream Analytics or Spark Structured Streaming
→ Synapse/Dedicated SQL for serving
example.walkthrough: Take 20 practice questions. For each, write the decision rule that picks the right service.

pitfalls: Studying services alphabetically — study by scenario (ingestion, batch, streaming, serving)
Ignoring cost/throughput limits — the exam loves 'which is cheapest that meets requirements'
No hands-on — scenario questions expose tutorial-only knowledge instantly
lessons.try_it: Build the decision matrix: rows=scenarios, columns=services, cells=when-to-pick.

lessons.title: Tricky Question Patterns
concepts: 'Least administrative effort' → managed/serverless options (Synapse serverless, ADF managed VNET)
'Minimize cost' → weigh provisioned vs serverless vs spot; storage tiering (Hot/Cool/Archive)
'Meet compliance' → Private Link, CMK, Purview — security answers hide in plain sight
Two right answers? Pick the one matching ALL constraints — re-read for the constraint you missed

example.code:
Q: 'Process 5TB nightly, minimize cost, 4hr window'
→ Wrong: always-on Databricks cluster
→ Right: ADF + Synapse serverless or job clusters
   (pay per job, not per hour)
example.walkthrough: Redo 10 missed questions. For each, name the constraint word that disambiguates the answer.

pitfalls: Answering from real-world habit instead of exam logic — the exam has its own preferences
Skipping the case study exhibits — answers hide in diagrams
Changing answers without reason — first instinct is right ~70% of the time
lessons.try_it: Create 5 'spot the constraint' flashcards from your misses. Drill until instant.

lessons.title: T-SQL for Data Engineers
concepts: Window functions (ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG/LEAD, SUM OVER) solve 80% of data-engineering SQL — learn them cold
CTEs structure complex logic readably; temp tables materialize for reuse across steps
Set-based thinking: describe the result set, not the loop — SQL is declarative
Distribution awareness on Synapse: hash vs round-robin vs replicated — wrong choice = data movement hell

example.code:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
    PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC) AS rn
  FROM orders)
SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1;  -- latest order per customer
example.walkthrough: Write 5 window-function queries: latest-per-group, running total, period-over-period, dedup, gaps.

pitfalls: Cursors/loops in T-SQL — set-based rewrites are 100x faster
SELECT * in production pipelines — schema drift breaks everything downstream
No distribution key thought on Synapse — shuffles on every join
lessons.try_it: Optimize a slow query: check the plan, fix the distribution, verify the improvement.

lessons.title: Dimensional Modeling & Medallion
concepts: Star schema: facts (measurements, FKs) + dimensions (descriptive) — optimized for analytic queries
SCD Type 1 (overwrite) vs Type 2 (history with effective dates) — choose by 'do we need the past?'
Medallion: Bronze (raw) → Silver (cleaned/conformed) → Gold (business-ready) — each layer has a contract
Surrogate keys decouple from source systems — source keys change; your warehouse shouldn't break

example.code:
-- SCD2 pattern
-- effective_from/to + is_current flag
-- new version on change, expire the old
-- history preserved, current = WHERE is_current = 1
example.walkthrough: Design a star schema for an orders domain: identify facts, dimensions, grain, and one SCD2 dimension.

pitfalls: Modeling the source schema 1:1 — OLTP shapes make terrible analytics
No conformed dimensions — every fact table redefines 'customer' differently
Skipping the silver layer — gold built directly on raw = untestable
lessons.try_it: Draw the medallion flow for a dataset you know. Define each layer's contract explicitly.

lessons.title: Performance Tuning on Azure
concepts: Partition pruning: partition by the filter column — queries that skip partitions are 10-100x faster
File sizing: ~128MB-1GB Parquet files; too many small files = metadata overhead death
Synapse: right distribution key eliminates shuffles; result-set caching for repeated dashboards
ADF: parallelize with ForEach batch count; tune DIUs for data flows — defaults are rarely optimal

example.walkthrough: Find a skewed table. Measure query time, change distribution, re-measure. Document the delta.

pitfalls: No partition elimination — full scans billed on every query
Small-file syndrome in the lake — thousands of KB files
Tuning compute before data layout — layout is usually the bigger lever
lessons.try_it: Run a data-flow with default vs tuned settings. Record cost and duration for both.

lessons.title: Data Engineering Projects That Prove It
concepts: End-to-end pipeline: ingest → bronze/silver/gold → serve — with the medallion layers actually implemented
Use the free tier smartly: Azurite/ADLS emulator + local Spark, or a cost-capped Azure sub with auto-shutdown
Document decisions: why Event Hubs over IoT Hub, why Delta over plain Parquet — decision records impress
Include a cost analysis — data engineers who think about money get hired faster

example.code:

# Retail Pipeline
## Architecture: [diagram]
## Layers: bronze/silver/gold contracts
## Cost: ~$X/month at Y scale
## Decisions: [ADR links]
example.walkthrough: Cost out your pipeline at 3 scales (dev/demo/prod). The exercise reveals design tradeoffs.

pitfalls: Notebook-only project — no orchestration, no scheduling, not a pipeline
No data quality checks — production pipelines validate; toys don't
Fake data with no documented grain — reviewers can't tell what's real
lessons.try_it: Add one data-quality gate (Great Expectations or custom) to your pipeline. Show a failing run.

simulations.title: The copy that keeps failing
simulations.brief: The nightly copy activity fails at 02:00 every night. The error mentions the source, not the sink. Work it.

steps.symptom: Copy activity fails nightly with a source connectivity error; the sink is healthy.
evidence:
Copy activity 'copy_customers' started 02:00
ERROR: source timeout after 30s — on-premises SQL Server unreachable
Sink: OK (not attempted)
options: Check the self-hosted integration runtime and the on-premises network path — the source is unreachable
Increase the sink's throughput — it must be the bottleneck
Rewrite the query — the SQL must be wrong
steps.explain: The error names the source side: timeout reaching the on-premises server. The self-hosted integration runtime and its network path are the suspects — the sink never even ran.

steps.symptom: The integration runtime host was patched and rebooted at 01:55 nightly.
options: Move the patch window off the pipeline's schedule and add a retry policy
Remove the integration runtime — go direct
Run the pipeline at noon instead
Accept the nightly failure — patches matter more
steps.explain: The patch window collides with the pipeline. Move the window (or the schedule) and add retries for transient blips. Removing the runtime breaks hybrid connectivity entirely.

simulations.debrief: You troubleshot at the right layer: the error named the source, the logs named the patch window. Fix the collision, don't redesign the pipeline.

simulations.title: Lake, warehouse, or lakehouse?
simulations.brief: Three workloads, three storage answers. Let the access pattern decide.

steps.text: Workload 1: analysts run ad-hoc SQL over 5 years of clickstream, schema evolves monthly. Store it where?

choices.label: Data warehouse with strict schema — cleanest
choices.feedback: A strict warehouse schema on monthly-evolving clickstream means constant ETL breakage.

choices.label: Data lake (raw) with schema-on-read — absorbs evolution
choices.feedback: Correct — volatile, exploratory data belongs in the lake with schema applied at read time.

steps.text: The ETL broke twice this month on new fields. Reconsider:

choices.label: Data lake with schema-on-read
choices.feedback: Right — let the lake absorb the volatility.

steps.text: Workload 2: finance close reporting, audited, must reconcile to the cent. Same answer?

choices.label: Yes — lake for everything, consistency
choices.feedback: Audited financial reporting needs curated, validated, schema-enforced data — the lake alone is not enough.

choices.label: No — curated warehouse tables with enforced schema and lineage
choices.feedback: Correct — regulated reporting gets the warehouse treatment: schema-on-write, validation, lineage.

simulations.debrief: You chose storage by workload: exploratory data in the lake, regulated reporting in the warehouse. The pattern decides, not preference.

simulations.title: The pipeline that silently drops rows
simulations.brief: Row counts drift between source and sink every night. Review the copy activity config and click the lines losing data.

steps.config:
Copy activity: copy_orders
1. Source: on-prem SQL, query: SELECT * FROM orders
2. Fault tolerance: skip incompatible rows
3. Logging: disabled
4. Sink: lake parquet, overwrite
5. Retry: 0

issues.description: 'Skip incompatible rows' silently drops rows that fail conversion — the drift source.
issues.fix: Route incompatible rows to a dead-letter path and alert; never silently skip.

issues.description: Logging disabled means the skipped rows leave no trace — undiagnosable drift.
issues.fix: Enable logging of skipped rows so data quality can be measured and fixed.

simulations.debrief: You found the silent-drop pattern: skip-plus-no-logging makes data disappear without a trace. Dead-letter and log, always.

sections.heading: Data Storage Design
items: ADLS Gen2 — ADLS Gen2's hierarchical namespace brings true directories with atomic renames — which Spark and Hadoop rely on for commit protocols.
Parquet's columnar layout — means queries read only needed columns (massive scan reduction); Delta Lake adds ACID transactions, schema enforcement, and time travel on top.
Partitioning — Partitioning organizes data so the engine prunes (skips) partitions outside the filter — a month query reads 1/60th of 5 years.
Common trap — deleting raw data after 90 days.
Common trap — manual tier changes quarterly.

Read — Read the setup and name the principle at play before looking at the reasoning. Then compare your answer with the takeaway — if they differ, re-read the concepts above and try the drill scenarios for this domain.

sections.heading: Data Factory
items: Linked — Linked services encapsulate connection information (server, auth via managed identity/Key Vault) as reusable named resources. Parameters let one pipeline definition run anywhere: linked services and datasets take parameters resolved at runtime or deploy time.
Integration runtimes — the self-hosted integration runtime runs inside your network and initiates outbound connections to Data Factory — no inbound firewall rules.

SSIS IR — azure IR handles cloud sources; SSIS IR lifts SSIS packages. The SSIS IR provisions the SSIS engine in ADF so existing packages run with minimal change — the pragmatic bridge while teams modernize package by package.

Lift-and-shift ETL — mapping data flows give a visual designer for joins, aggregations, window functions, and schema handling, executed on ADF-managed Spark — ETL for teams that think in diagrams, with code (wraggle/data flow script) underneath.
Common trap — copying the JSON fifty times.
Common trap — rewriting all 300 as ADF pipelines immediately.

sections.heading: Synapse & Databricks
items: Synapse pools — serverless SQL pools charge per data scanned with zero provisioning — ideal for sporadic analyst queries over lake files. Dedicated SQL pools provision compute (DWUs) for consistent, heavy relational workloads — the classic data warehouse.
Dedicated vs serverless — serverless is pay-per-TB-scanned for ad-hoc queries over the lake; neither replaces the other. Running dedicated capacity for a few queries a week is pure waste.
Broadcast — Broadcast joins replicate the small table to every executor so the big table isn't shuffled — the standard fix for fact-to-small-dimension joins.
Common trap — dedicated SQL pool running 24/7.
Common trap — copying Parquet into SQL Server.
Common trap — a batch job listing everything hourly.
Common trap — repartitioning the fact table randomly.

sections.heading: Stream Processing

Consumer — Consumer groups give each downstream app an independent view (own offsets) of the same partitions — the dashboard reads real-time while the archive lags, neither blocking the other.

Stream Analytics windows (tumbling — non-overlapping; hopping: overlapping; sliding; session) bound aggregations in event time. Stream systems define lateness policies: how far behind event time you'll still accept data.

sections.heading: Security
items: Managed identity — aDF's system-assigned managed identity authenticates to Azure data stores via RBAC — no credentials to rotate, expire, or leak. ADF needs a managed VNet/IR or private endpoints to reach it — network design is part of data security.
Private endpoints — data-plane privacy needs private endpoints (lake traffic stays in the VNet) plus public-access disabled at the account level.

Data network security — revoking the key renders the data unreadable — the contractual 'we control the keys' proof. Purview's scanners classify sensitive data (emails, SSNs, etc.) across ADLS, SQL, and more, building a searchable data map — the only feasible answer at lake scale u…
CMK moves key — control (creation, rotation, revocation) to your Key Vault while the service still performs encryption.
Skipping the key question — how do pipelines authenticate with zero stored secrets.
Skipping the key question — how do you make lake traffic never touch the public internet.

sections.heading: Monitoring
items: ADF monitoring — production pipelines must expect schema change: ADF data flows support schema drift; Delta Lake supports schema evolution/merging. ADF emits run metrics and diagnostic logs; alert rules on failed pipeline/activity runs (via action groups) notify immediately.
Alert rules — cluster policies constrain allowed sizes and auto-terminate idle clusters; budgets alert on spend.
Synapse Monitor — the Monitor hub surfaces executed queries with durations, queued time, DWU usage, and distribution skew — the evidence for 'concurrency vs. skew vs. bad query'.
Log delivery — clusters are ephemeral; without log delivery, driver/executor logs vanish on termination.

checklist: Get 7–8 hours of sleep the night before — fatigue destroys recall faster than any topic gap.
Bring valid government-issued photo ID and arrive at the test center 30 minutes early.
Eat a real meal beforehand; bring water and a light snack if the center allows them.
Read every question twice before scanning the answer choices.
Flag uncertain questions and move on — return with fresh eyes at the end.
Eliminate the obviously wrong answers first, then compare the survivors.
Budget your time: answer steadily and keep a 10–15 minute review buffer.
Re-run your weakest-domain drill until mastery is at least 80%.
